analysis.title: AI rout: Our view
key_insights: Global equities fell sharply, led by AI, semiconductor and data-centre-related companies. Fidelity calls the sell-off technically driven and says it followed sweeping Democratic gains in the US midterm elections.

Democratic wins in Texas, Ohio and Georgia raised concerns about tighter permitting and construction delays for data centres. These states are important to planned US AI infrastructure investment, so the pace of the capex cycle is in question.

Fidelity says the size of the move appears amplified by crowded positioning, leveraged investors and options-related hedging. Technical selling of this size has historically left markets oversold and created opportunities to add exposure.
The current AI cycle is driven mainly by capital expenditure rather than consumer spending, so it needs financing to keep its pace. This makes it more sensitive to a technically driven sell-off.

A slowdown in AI capex could weigh on headline GDP growth, since AI drives growth directly through investment demand and indirectly through equity-rally wealth effects on consumer demand. That could support a further rally in bonds, which have already moved higher on hopes of a calmer Middle East.
Near term, the financing needs of the capex cycle and technical factors mean volatility could stay elevated, and Fidelity says this needs to be reflected in portfolio construction.

Medium to long term, Fidelity expects healthy earnings growth over the next two years, supported by a global economy still in expansion. Higher rates and volatility have compressed valuation multiples, leaving some higher-quality companies at attractive valuations.

Fidelity expects the next phase of the AI cycle to favour higher-quality companies with easier access to financing. Opportunities should broaden toward companies adopting AI rather than those focused purely on capex.

Fidelity has reduced and adjusted its AI and technology positioning in recent months. It is keeping positions smaller, assessing markets technically, and looking to add exposure to higher-quality companies.

Minimum volatility stocks have rallied. Since the start of October 2026, European minimum volatility indices are up more than 12% while broad global indices are down more than 2%, and some consumer staples stocks are up more than 20%. Fidelity reads this as rotation within equities rather than a broad withdrawal, with hedge fund liquidations likely adding to volatility.
Some of the rotation areas look overbought in the short term, and Europe may face additional headwinds in 2027.

Gold has held up relatively well. If the AI investment cycle slows, Fidelity says the recent downtrend in gold could reverse, given the market backdrop, government bond developments, the AI trade and already lighter positioning.

Fidelity cut overall risk exposure from overweight to neutral in September and remains neutral. It sees no indicators pointing to the end of the economic cycle, but uncertainty around interest rates and the Middle East could keep volatility high. It also flags the risk that volatility becomes self-reinforcing given the financing the AI capex cycle needs.

tension_points.bull_case: Fidelity says the longer-term structural case for AI remains compelling, with healthy two-year earnings growth, compressed multiples and technically oversold conditions that may offer chances to add exposure.
tension_points.bear_case: Democratic gains could bring tighter data-centre permitting and construction delays, and the capex-driven cycle depends on financing. Volatility could become self-reinforcing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Slower AI capex that weighs on headline GDP growth, or tighter regulation and permitting on data-centre development in key states such as Texas, Ohio and Georgia.
